items.title: Jamey Aebersold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 26, 2022
items.q: Benny Golson has one [CD in the play-a-long series]

ctx.x: Oh that’s priceless. Well you’ve had your share of technological changes and challenges because you’ve been in business so long. I recall the fellow that used to run Commodore Records talking about when 78s changed over to LPs and what a — it almost put them out of business because they had all this stock. How do you — did you see the CD thing coming?

Yeah but we put it off for a while. Getting up the cassettes was good but the problem with cassettes were they didn’t always run at the same speed. I don’t know if you remember or not but let me just think a second — SONY had a cassette player. Yeah that’s what it was. And it had a pitch control on it. Yes. And it was great for play-a-longs. It was a cassette player with a pitch control. But then I think they found out it probably cost them ten cents to put that on there but they found out that the only people…
So the accompaniments that came with the book that’s over my shoulder, you took them and digitally they were able to be slowed down, is that correct?

items.title: Aebersold Jamey — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

ctx.x: There you’ve got Volume 6 with Charlie Parker, and then Miles Davis, Sonny Rollins and Woody Shaw.

Incidentally, the Volume 1, the Volume 3, the Volume 6... Volume 14—Benny Golson. Volume 17—Horace Silver. Volume 18—Horace Silver. We, as of the last year or two...we have slowed those records down, those Play-A-Longs, and now they have two CDs— slower tempos and original tempos. Because jazz education has moved through the years down and down age-wise, so you’ve got 10-, 11- and 12-, 13-year-old people trying to play Volume 1, our Charlie Parker tunes, our Horace Silver tunes. So we’ve been able to digitally…
And was it pitch control...not pitch control...
